chunks: From him, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ḥadhdhāʾ, who said:
I was with Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام when a man asked me, “What did your adversary do?”
I said, “That son of the fornicatress.” So Abū ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام looked at me sternly. He said: Then I said, “May I be your ransom, he is a Magian; his mother is his sister.”
So he said, “Is that not, in their religion, a marriage?”

key_terms.دِينِهِمْ: their religion, meaning the religious law or custom they follow
key_terms.غَرِيمُكَ: your adversary or opponent in a dispute
key_terms.مَجُوسِيٌّ: a Magian, referring to a follower of the Magian religion
key_terms.نَظَرًا شَدِيدًا: a stern look expressing strong disapproval
key_terms.نِكَاحًا: marriage, regarded here as a legally recognized union within their religion
key_terms.ٱبْنُ ٱلْفَاعِلَةِ: an insulting expression meaning son of a fornicatress

ai.seo_question: Can a person be blamed with an insulting accusation based on a marriage considered valid in their own religion?
ai.summary: This hadith teaches restraint in insult and false disparagement, even toward an opponent. Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام reproves using a sexually defamatory insult against a Magian on the basis of a relationship considered marriage in that community’s religion. The report has ethical and legal significance in matters of slander, abuse, and how accusations are judged.
